summary: Leave It Behind is a free 2D browser game that tells the story of the hardware NASA left on the Moon by making players face the same choice Apollo crews did. You land at a real Apollo site (Apollo 11, 12 or 17), collect rock samples, core tubes and film, and set up experiments like the laser retroreflector that scientists still use today. The catch: your ascent stage has a weight limit, and the cabin is already full of gear. To lift off, you must throw out backpacks, boots and cameras, just as the real crews did, which is why those objects are still on the Moon. After liftoff, reentry and splashdown, you hand your samples to scientists at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Houston, and each sample you brought home unlocks the discovery it made possible. Every object shows a short, kid-friendly fact, linking each piece of hardware to its science. For school-age space fans, it turns discarded equipment into decisions they make themselves, and it carries a lesson for life: sometimes you have to lose something to make something.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: Leave It Behind is a free 2D side-scrolling game that runs in any browser, on phones, tablets and laptops. Players land on three real Apollo sites: Apollo 11 (Tranquility Base), Apollo 12 (Ocean of Storms, where you walk to the 1967 Surveyor 3 lander and bring its camera home) and Apollo 17 (Taurus-Littrow, with its orange volcanic soil). In low gravity, they collect rock samples, core tubes and film, and carry instruments such as the laser retroreflector and seismometer to their marked sites. Instruments only score if they are left behind and working, which shows why some of this hardware still matters today.

HOW IT WORKS: The lunar module's ascent stage has a weight limit, and the cabin starts full of gear. To lift off, players must throw out backpacks, boots, cameras and tools, exactly as Apollo crews did. That is why these objects are on NASA's Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon. Too heavy, and the engine cannot lift off. Oxygen runs on a timer. After a successful liftoff, a short cinematic shows the trip home, reentry, parachutes, splashdown and recovery. Players then deliver their samples to the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Houston, where each sample they brought home unlocks the discovery it made possible. The results screen compares their choices with what the real crew did.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT: Space content for kids often skips the engineering trade-offs or explains them at a level that loses young learners. Here the trade-off is the game. Students feel why every kilogram matters, learn what each object did and what science it enabled, and take away a life lesson: sometimes you have to lose something to make something. It fits a 20-minute classroom activity and needs no install. Next steps: Mars missions (Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity), real LROC and HiRISE orbital views of each site, an Arabic and English toggle, and pilots with UAE schools.

TOOLS: HTML5 canvas and plain JavaScript (no frameworks, no build step), keyboard and touch controls, Web Audio for sound, GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. Source code: https://github.com/Saloom-Inc/nasa. All art is original vector drawing in code; no NASA logos, insignia or mission patches are used. Built with Claude (Anthropic) as a Super Intelligence tool, as disclosed in the README, the game's About screen and the watermark on the demo video. Weights in the game are simplified units; mission facts are based on NASA sources.
